findings.source_passage: Oh! he's a wonderful old man!
findings.why_it_matters: Stubb's exclamation is a small but tonally distinct voice-marker that establishes the crew's awed admiration of Ahab; its omission flattens Stubb's characterization and the chapter's opening register.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the exclamation at the close of Stubb's speech: 'Oh! he's a wonderful old man!'

findings.source_passage: I don't know that, my little man; I never yet saw him kneel.
findings.why_it_matters: This dry, ironic one-liner is a textually distinctive and critically noted witticism that encapsulates the novel's irreverent treatment of Ahab's disability; losing it removes a recognizable Stubb voice-moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Stubb's rejoinder verbatim after Flask's anatomical reasoning.

findings.source_passage: now and then such unaccountable odds and ends of strange nations come up from the unknown nooks and ash-holes of the earth to man these floating outlaws of whalers
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Now, with the subordinate phantoms'
findings.why_it_matters: The rhetorically charged phrase 'unknown nooks and ash-holes of the earth' is signature Melville diction—visceral, irreverent, and globally suggestive; the draft reduces it to 'outlandish odds and ends of nations ever come up,' stripping the voice-defining imagery.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the source phrasing 'from the unknown nooks and ash-holes of the earth' in the forecastle paragraph.

summary: The draft preserves all high-priority signatures intact, including the full Fedallah description and the Tamerlane comparison, but loses three medium-weight Stubb voice-moments and one stretch of signature Melvillean diction, none individually severe enough to require regeneration.
